summary: An April 1st joke RFC that proposes reaching "infinite bandwidth" in IP networks through ESP-based forwarding, where ESP stands for Extra Sensory Perception: packets are forwarded by psychic means. It is not the IPsec security protocol of the same initials, and the document should be read as humor rather than a real engineering proposal.

eli5.summary: Someone wrote a joke recipe claiming you can make a road with endless lanes by using a special trick. Nobody should expect the trick to work; it is just for a laugh.

questions: can ip networks have infinite bandwidth
subtitle: An April 1st proposal for reaching infinite bandwidth using psychic forwarding

tldr.problem: Despite decades of optimization, network latency is limited by the speed of light, and demand for bandwidth always exceeds capacity.
tldr.mechanism: ESP-Based Forwarding uses precognitive packet generation to forward packets before they arrive, eliminating end-to-end latency through fictional quantum and psychic mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st joke document; none of the techniques are real. The fictional proposal uses imaginary components like the Infinite Improbability Drive (from Douglas Adams) and Ouija boards for routing.

today: RFC 5984 is an April 1st humor document published on 1 April 2011. It proposes no real protocol or implementation and should not be treated as a serious engineering proposal. The document itself acknowledges that the Pre-Preemptive Scheduler will always be slightly ahead of its time, making the product unmarketable. It is listed as Experimental but is fiction, not an implementable specification.

sections.title: The April Fools Premise
sections.content:
This is an April 1st RFC, published on 1 April 2011. It is a humor document and should be read as fiction, not engineering advice. The entire proposal is tongue-in-cheek.

The RFC purports to solve a real network problem (latency and capacity growth) with entirely fictional mechanisms. It proposes ESP-Based Forwarding (where ESP means Extra Sensory Perception, not the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload), which would use precognitive packet generation to achieve zero or negative latency.

The document references failed experimental approaches: attempts using black fiber and Schrödinger's cat experiment, both presented with absurdist humor.
sections.eli5: The author is telling jokes about trying ridiculous things like black fiber (fiber with no light) and cat experiments to make the internet faster, then proposing an even more ridiculous solution using psychic powers.

sections.title: Core Fictional Concepts
sections.content:
The document invokes real physics and philosophy to frame its humor:

  • Speed of light limitation: Correctly notes RFC 1925 clause 2, which humorously states that the speed of light cannot be exceeded no matter the effort. The proposal claims to circumvent this by achieving zero-latency paths.
  • Infinite Improbability Drive (IID): References Douglas Adams' Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. The RFC seriously describes the IID as helping with improbable calculations, mentioning the fictional Bambleweeny 57 sub-meson Brain and requiring a Brownian motion producer (a warm cup of tea, later replaced with a hovercraft full of eels).
  • Readiness potential: References Benjamin Libet's neuroscience experiments on conscious will, claiming a 350-400 ms latency between impulse and conscious awareness, which the system must accommodate.
sections.eli5: The author uses real science (speed of light, brain latency) mixed with obvious jokes (magic drives, eels, Ouija boards) to create a funny fake engineering proposal.

sections.title: Fictional Architecture and Components
sections.content:
The ESP-Based Forwarding system nominally includes these fictional components:

  • DPAUI (Deep Packet And User Inspection): Monitors data streams to predict when users will send packets.
  • PPG (Precognitive Packet Generator): Generates future packets by looking up their bit patterns in the infinite decimal expansion of pi (stored in a circular buffer to save space).
  • IID (Infinite Improbability Drive): Assists with improbable calculations; the RFC comically describes failed implementations using warm tea and eels.
  • CFE (Clairvoyant Forwarding Engine): Routes packets using a standard routing table covered with a Ouija board to consult routing daemons about the packet's future path.
  • PPS (Pre-Preemptive Scheduler): Executes code ten seconds into the future using string theory and eleven-dimensional arrays via strcpy.
  • ND (Null Device): Discards the real user datagram after the precognitive copy has already been forwarded.
sections.eli5: The author invents fake computer parts with silly names and describes their operation in overly technical language to make the joke convincing.

sections.title: End User and Market Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC humorously addresses deployment challenges:

  • Gaming: User spinal cord packets (force feedback) must be delayed by 350 ms to synchronize with packets reaching the brain, based on Libet's readiness potential research.
  • Bad news travels fast: RFC 1216 supposedly states that bad news travels faster. Additional delay is added to news sites so users do not suspect the news is worse than indicated.
  • Machine-to-Machine (M2M): The DPAUI fails for M2M communication, and successful M2M performance would indicate a technological singularity.
  • Market viability: The RFC concludes that the Pre-Preemptive Scheduler will always be slightly ahead of its time, so the product will never be ready for the market.
sections.eli5: The author adds silly requirements (syncing with brain latency, special handling for bad news) and jokes about why the product would never actually work.
